Alanine dosimetry measures stable free radicals produced by ionizing radiation detected via ESR.
The Fricke dosimetry system uses ferrous ammonium sulfate solution to measure absorbed dose chemically.
The optical density increase at 304 nm corresponds to the conversion of Fe2+ to Fe3+ ions.
Electron beams from 5.3 to 22.4 MeV were used, with clinical relevance focused on 6 to 20 MeV.
A 22 MeV microtron accelerator with a conventional treatment head was the radiation source.
The Fricke solution calibration factor G is independent of electron energy within uncertainties.
Total absorption of the electron beam in a glass vessel filled with Fricke solution allows absolute dose measurement.
Monte Carlo simulations correct for energy losses due to backscattering, Bremsstrahlung, and absorption upstream.
Alanine dosimeters were irradiated in a water phantom at a reference depth defined by z_ref = 0.6 × R_50 − 0.1 g/cm².
Secondary standard ionization chambers calibrated against Fricke dosimetry provide dose reference during alanine irradiation.
No significant energy dependence of alanine dosimeter response was found between 6 and 20 MeV electrons.
A unique correction factor k_E = 1.012 ± 0.010 is recommended for alanine dosimetry in MeV electron beams.
Corrections for temperature differences during irradiation and optical density measurement are applied.
Polyethylene bags used to hold Fricke solution are corrected for possible oxidation effects.
The magnetic spectrometer used for beam energy measurement has a 180° bending magnet and Faraday cup detector.
The pulse frequency of the accelerator during total absorption experiments was reduced to 1 Hz to avoid high local dose rates.
The Fricke solution's absorbed dose is proportional to the number of incident electrons and their mean energy.
The study confirms alanine dosimetry suitability for quality assurance in modern radiotherapy involving megavoltage electrons.
The Fricke dosimetry system at METAS has been established for over 10 years.
The study provides a detailed description of the Fricke primary standard measurement system not previously published.
